module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Ben Green's Open Problem 82

*References:*
- [Ben Green's Open Problem 82](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.82)
- [An improved lower bound for a problem of Littlewood on the zeros of cosine polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16075) (Bedert, 2025)
- [Cosine polynomials with few zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.01695) (Juškevičius & Sahasrabudhe, 2020)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter Real Set
open scoped Finset

namespace Green82

/-- The minimum number of zeros in $[0,1)$ of $\sum_{a \in A} \cos(2\pi a\theta)$
over all sets $A \subset \mathbb{Z}$ of size $n$. -/
noncomputable def minZeros (n : ℕ+) : ℕ∞ :=
  ⨅ A : {A : Finset ℤ // A.card = n},
    ({θ : ℝ | θ ∈ Ico 0 1 ∧ ∑ a ∈ A.val, cos (2 * π * a * θ) = 0} : Set ℝ).ncard

/-- Let $A \subset \mathbb{Z}$ be a set of size $n$. For how many $\theta \in \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$
must we have $\sum_{a \in A} \cos(2\pi a\theta) = 0$? The answer is the function `minZeros`. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11 42]
theorem green_82 : (answer(sorry) : ℕ+ → ℕ∞) = minZeros := by
  sorry

/-- Lower bound: every set has at least $(\log \log n)^{1-o(1)}$ zeros. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 42]
theorem green_82_lower_bound :
    ∃ o : ℕ → ℝ, o =o[atTop] (fun _ ↦ (1 : ℝ)) ∧
      ∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∀ A : Finset ℤ, A.card = n →
        (⌊(Real.log (Real.log n)) ^ (1 - |o n|)⌋₊ : ℕ∞) ≤
        ({θ : ℝ | θ ∈ Ico 0 1 ∧ ∑ a ∈ A, cos (2 * π * a * θ) = 0} : Set ℝ).ncard := by
  sorry

/-- Upper bound: there exists $A$ with at most $C(n \log n)^{2/3}$ zeros. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 42]
theorem green_82_upper_bound :
    ∃ C > 0, ∀ n ≥ 1, ∃ A : Finset ℤ, A.card = n ∧
      ({θ : ℝ | θ ∈ Ico 0 1 ∧ ∑ a ∈ A, cos (2 * π * a * θ) = 0} : Set ℝ).ncard ≤
      (⌊C * (n * Real.log n) ^ (2 / 3 : ℝ)⌋₊ : ℕ∞) := by
  sorry

end Green82

reformulations.difference: The source counts angles on the circle, while Lean counts representatives in [0,1), normalizes the cosine argument by 2π, and expresses the minimum as an ℕ∞-valued infimum of natural cardinalities.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The normalized sum is 1-periodic, so [0,1) represents each circle point exactly once. Substituting t = 2πθ gives the papers' usual period. For positive-sized A, both endpoints have value |A| > 0, so including the right endpoint would not add a zero. The sum is analytic and nonzero at 0; hence its zeros in the bounded period are finite and Set.ncard has its ordinary cardinality meaning. There are integer sets of every positive size, and the infimum of this nonempty family of natural counts is attained. Periodicity, finiteness, endpoint behavior, and attainment were checked in Lean; the full quotient identification was not formalized.

reformulations.difference: Lean writes the asymptotic lower bound using an explicit o = o(1), the exponent 1 - |o n|, and a natural-number floor.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Little-o of the constant 1 means convergence to zero. Taking the absolute value does not change an existential asymptotic lower bound: it can only decrease the exponent once L = log log n > 1. Rounding is also immaterial. With t = L^(1-|o n|), we have t → ∞ and eventually floor(t) ≥ t/2. The factor 1/2 is absorbed by replacing the exponent error with |o n| + log(2)/log(L), which still tends to zero. Conversely, an unrounded lower bound implies the rounded one after replacing its error by its absolute value. Thus the statement is equivalent to the source's (log log n)^(1-o(1)) lower bound.

review.notes: Checked all four declarations. The cited sources support the main problem's open status and both bounds' solved status. Bedert's general finite-coefficient theorem covers A ⊆ ℤ: combining opposite frequencies gives coefficients in {0,1,2}, with value |A| at zero. The scratch file /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles successfully and verifies, among other checks, finiteness of the zero sets, attainment of minZeros, minZeros 1 = 0, and the upper bound's singleton case using A = {0}. Thus log 1 = 0 does not invalidate the upper bound. No mathematical defects found.
